passages.happening:
Paul stands on the steps of the Roman barracks, in chains, facing the crowd that has just tried to kill him. He begins, “Brothers and fathers, listen now to my defense before you” (verse 1). When they hear him speaking in Hebrew, they grow even quieter (verse 2).

“I am a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but raised in this city,” he says. He was “educated at the feet of Gamaliel in strict conformity to the law of our fathers”, and he is “just as zealous for God as any of you here today” (verse 3). He persecuted “this Way” to the death, putting men and women in prison (verse 4). The high priest and the whole Council can say so. He even carried their letters to Damascus, to arrest believers there and bring them back to Jerusalem to be punished (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Paul's opening words, ‘Brothers and fathers’, are the respectful greeting of one Jew to an assembly of his own people. Stephen began the same way before the Council (7:2). Paul is not speaking as an outsider attacking them. He is speaking as one of them.

The language matters too. ‘In Hebrew’ may mean the Hebrew language or Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in Judea; scholars differ, as the note on 21:37-40 says. Either way, the commander had just heard Paul speak educated Greek. Now Paul turns to the crowd and speaks to them in the language of home, and they fall silent.

He tells them three things about himself. He was born in Tarsus, a proud city of the Greek-speaking world, but ‘raised in this city’, Jerusalem. He was taught by Gamaliel. Gamaliel was a leading Pharisee, ‘honored by all the people’ (5:34). Jewish tradition remembers a great teacher called Rabban Gamaliel the Elder; the Mishnah says that when he died, the glory of the law ceased. Most identify him with the Gamaliel of Acts. To ‘sit at the feet’ of a teacher meant to be his pupil. And Paul was zealous: so zealous that he hunted down the followers of Jesus.

‘The Way’ is one of the earliest names for the followers of Jesus (9:2), and Paul uses it here before a crowd that thinks he has betrayed Israel. His point is simple. Everything they feel about him now, he once felt about the believers. He understands their anger from the inside. He does not mock their zeal. He shares it, and he tells them where his own zeal led him.
passages.ot:
Paul's zeal has a long history in Israel. Phinehas was praised because “he was zealous for his God” (Numbers 25:13), and Elijah said, “I have been very zealous for the LORD, the God of Hosts” (1 Kings 19:10). Zeal for God was a good thing in Israel's Scriptures. Paul's story is about what happens when that zeal is aimed at the wrong target.

His love for ‘the law of our fathers’ is the love of the Psalms: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105).
passages.asks: Paul did not begin by attacking the crowd. He began with everything he shared with them: language, city, teacher, zeal. Ask whether, when you speak about your faith to people who are angry with it, you start with what you have in common. And ask whether you have ever been certain and wrong, as Paul was, and what it took to turn you.

passages.t: The light at noon, told a second time
passages.happening:
“About noon as I was approaching Damascus,” Paul says, “suddenly a bright light from heaven flashed around me” (verse 6). He fell to the ground and heard a voice: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” (verse 7). He asked who was speaking, and the answer came, “I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting” (verse 8).

His companions saw the light but “could not understand the voice of the One speaking to me” (verse 9). Paul asked what he should do, and the Lord told him to go into Damascus, where he would be told everything he had been appointed to do (verse 10). Blinded by the light, he was led by the hand into the city (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
This is the second of three tellings of the same event in Acts. Luke tells it himself in chapter 9, Paul tells it here to a Jewish crowd, and Paul tells it again before King Agrippa in chapter 26. The tellings differ in small ways. The note on Acts 9:1-9 sets out how readers account for them, including the question of whether the companions heard the voice (9:7) or could not understand it (verse 9 here). These notes do not repeat that discussion here.

Notice what Paul adds for this crowd. It was ‘about noon’, the brightest hour of the day, and still the light was brighter. And Jesus names himself as ‘Jesus of Nazareth’, the plain name of a man from a small town in Galilee, the man this city had seen crucified. For a Jerusalem crowd, that was the shock. The voice from heaven was the voice of the man they knew had died.

Paul also tells it as a story of being stopped. He was riding out with authority and letters. He arrived blind, led by the hand. He does not make himself a hero. The proud persecutor is the one who had to be helped into the city.
passages.ot: A man struck down before the glory of God is an old picture in Scripture. When Ezekiel saw the likeness of the LORD's glory, he wrote, “I fell facedown and heard a voice speaking” (Ezekiel 1:28). When God called Moses by name from the bush, he called him twice: “Moses, Moses!” (Exodus 3:4). So too he called “Samuel, Samuel!” (1 Samuel 3:10). The double name here, ‘Saul, Saul’, sounds like the call of a prophet.
passages.asks: Paul told the worst thing about himself, that he persecuted Jesus, to people who could use it against him. Ask whether you can tell your own story honestly, including the parts you are ashamed of. And notice that the risen Jesus said, ‘You are persecuting Me.’ Ask what it means that Jesus counts the way his people are treated as the way he is treated.

passages.happening:
In Damascus, Paul says, a man named Ananias came to him. Ananias was “a devout observer of the law who was highly regarded by all the Jews living there” (verse 12). He stood beside Paul, called him ‘Brother Saul’, and told him to receive his sight, and at that moment Paul could see (verse 13).

Ananias told him, “The God of our fathers has appointed you to know His will, and to see the Righteous One, and to hear His voice” (verse 14). Paul would be a witness to everyone of what he had seen and heard (verse 15). “And now what are you waiting for? Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
In chapter 9 Ananias is simply ‘a disciple’. Here Paul describes him the way this crowd would respect: a devout Jew who kept the law, well thought of by all the Jews in Damascus. Paul is not changing the facts; he is choosing which of them to tell. The man who welcomed him into the faith was exactly the kind of Jew his hearers admired.

Ananias speaks of ‘the God of our fathers’, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. He calls Jesus ‘the Righteous One’, the same title Peter (3:14) and Stephen (7:52) used. In this telling, there is no new God and no new religion. The God of Israel has shown Paul his Messiah.

Then comes verse 16: ‘Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name.’ Christians read this verse in different ways, as they do Peter's words at Pentecost (2:38). Some read it as teaching that God really washes away sin in baptism, received in faith. Others read it as teaching that sins are washed away by calling on the name of Jesus in faith, and that baptism is the outward sign and confession of that washing. The grammar of the verse is argued over too, since the washing could be tied to the baptism or to the calling on his name. The note on Acts 2:37-41 sets out the main readings of the churches in the words their holders would use. These notes do not choose between them. All agree that the cleansing comes from Christ, and that Paul was told not to wait.
passages.ot:
‘The God of our fathers’ is how God named himself to Moses: “the LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:15).

The picture of washing away sin runs through the Old Testament. David prayed, “Wash me clean of my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin” (Psalm 51:2), and Isaiah heard God say, “Wash and cleanse yourselves” (Isaiah 1:16). And calling on the name goes back to Joel: “everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved” (Joel 2:32), which Peter quoted at Pentecost (2:21).
passages.asks: Ananias went to the man who had come to arrest people like him, and called him ‘Brother’. Ask who would be hardest for you to call brother or sister. And Ananias asked, ‘What are you waiting for?’ Ask whether there is a step of obedience you already know you should take, and are putting off.

passages.t: In the temple: ‘I will send you far away’
passages.happening:
Paul goes on. Later, back in Jerusalem, he was praying in the temple when he fell into a trance (verse 17). He saw the Lord, who told him to leave Jerusalem quickly, “because the people here will not accept your testimony about Me” (verse 18).

Paul argued. The people knew he had imprisoned and beaten believers in synagogue after synagogue (verse 19). He had even stood by and approved when Stephen was killed, guarding the cloaks of those who stoned him (verse 20). Surely they would listen to a man like that. But the Lord said, “Go! I will send you far away to the Gentiles” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
This vision is told only here. Notice where it happens. Paul was not turning his back on the temple. He was praying there, in Israel's holiest place, when the Lord sent him to the nations. For a crowd that believed Paul had brought a Gentile into the temple and defiled it, this was a pointed answer. His mission to the Gentiles did not come from contempt for the temple. It came to him while he was worshipping in it.

Paul's argument with the Lord is very human. He thought his past would make his witness powerful in Jerusalem: everyone knew what he had been, so surely his change would convince them. The Lord said no. In chapter 9 the believers sent Paul away from Jerusalem because some there were trying to kill him (9:29-30). Here Paul tells the same departure from the inside: it was also the Lord's command.

Paul names Stephen, ‘Your witness’. He does not hide that he stood beside Stephen's killers. The word for witness here, martus, later came to mean martyr, someone who dies for the faith (the book page says more on this). Paul carries Stephen's death with him still.
passages.ot:
Isaiah too was in the temple when the Lord sent him: “Whom shall I send? Who will go for Us?” (Isaiah 6:8). And Isaiah too was told that the people would not listen (Isaiah 6:9-10), words Paul will quote at the very end of Acts (28:26-27).

The sending to the Gentiles was in Israel's own Scriptures. God told his servant, “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). Paul and Barnabas quoted that verse in Pisidian Antioch (13:47).
passages.asks: Paul thought his story would win his own city, and the Lord sent him somewhere else. Ask whether you are holding on to a plan for how God should use you, and whether you could let him send you somewhere you did not choose. And notice that Paul still carried Stephen's death. Ask what you carry from your past, and whether you have brought it to God.

passages.t: The crowd turns at one word
passages.happening:
“The crowd listened to Paul until he made this statement” (verse 22): the word that God had sent him to the Gentiles. Then they shout, “Rid the earth of him! He is not fit to live!” (verse 22). They throw off their cloaks and toss dust into the air (verse 23).

The commander has Paul brought into the barracks. He orders him to be flogged and questioned, to find out why the crowd is shouting against him (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Why did that one word, ‘Gentiles’, turn the crowd? It helps to hear it the way they heard it, without looking down on them.

They had just been told that Paul had brought a Gentile into the temple (21:28-29). That was false, but they believed it. Their nation lived under Gentile rule. Roman soldiers stood in a fortress beside God's house, and a Roman governor appointed their high priest. For many, faithfulness to God meant keeping Israel apart from the nations that ruled and mocked it. Now a man who admitted he had been a strict Pharisee was saying that God himself had sent him away from Jerusalem to the Gentiles, and was welcoming them in without asking them to become Jews. To them it sounded like the betrayal of everything their fathers had suffered to keep.

The Gentiles were never outside Israel's hope; the Old Testament note below shows that. But the crowd heard Paul's words through fear and the false report, and they exploded.

They throw off their cloaks and toss dust in the air. These were signs of fury and outrage; some readers think they also showed readiness to stone him, though that is not certain. Their cry, ‘Rid the earth of him’, is close to the cry that went up in this same city against Jesus (Luke 23:18), and against Paul a few days earlier (21:36).

This was one crowd in Jerusalem on one day, stirred by a false rumour. It was not the Jewish people. Thousands of Jews in this very city had believed in Jesus and loved the law (21:20). Paul, who speaks, is a Jew. The note on Acts 2:22-28 explains how scenes like this were later turned against the Jewish people, and why this site rejects that reading.

The commander, who probably could not follow Paul's Hebrew, sees only a riot. He decides to get the truth by whipping it out of his prisoner.
passages.ot:
The welcome of the nations was in Israel's Scriptures from the start. God told Abraham, “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). The prophets saw the nations coming to Israel's God: “Nations will come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn” (Isaiah 60:3). Even the temple was to be “a house of prayer for all the nations” (Isaiah 56:7).

A prophet whose people would not hear him is an old story too. When Jeremiah finished speaking in the LORD's house, the crowd said, “You must surely die” (Jeremiah 26:8).
passages.asks: The crowd listened until they heard the one thing they could not accept: God's welcome for people they feared. Ask which people you would find it hardest to hear God welcoming. And ask whether you have ever let a rumour you believed shape how you heard someone.

passages.happening:
As the soldiers stretch Paul out and strap him down, he says to the centurion standing by, “Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen without a trial?” (verse 25). The centurion goes straight to the commander. “What are you going to do?” he asks. “This man is a Roman citizen” (verse 26).

The commander comes and asks, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” Paul says yes (verse 27). The commander says, “I paid a high price for my citizenship.” Paul replies, “But I was born a citizen” (verse 28). The men about to question him step back, and the commander is alarmed that he has put a Roman citizen in chains (verse 29).

The next day, wanting to know the real charge, the commander releases Paul from his chains, orders the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin to meet, and brings Paul down to stand before them (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
The flogging the commander ordered was not the beating with rods Paul suffered at Philippi (16:22), nor the synagogue punishment of thirty-nine lashes (2 Corinthians 11:24). It was the Roman scourge: a whip of leather thongs, sometimes weighted with pieces of bone or metal. It was used to force the truth out of prisoners who were not citizens, and it could cripple or kill.

Roman citizenship was a legal standing, not a nationality, and in the eastern provinces only a minority held it. It came by birth, by grant from an emperor or general, by finishing service in the auxiliary army, or by being freed by a citizen master. It protected the body. A citizen was not to be flogged or bound without trial, and he could appeal against a magistrate's sentence. Paul waits until he is strapped down to ask his question, and the danger turns round. Now it is the officers who are in trouble.

The commander's reply is revealing. He ‘paid a high price’ for his citizenship. The Roman historian Cassius Dio says that under the emperor Claudius citizenship was sold through the empress Messalina and the freed slaves of the palace, dear at first and later very cheap. The commander's name, Claudius Lysias (23:26), fits a man who took the emperor's name when he became a citizen, though that is an inference.

Paul was ‘born a citizen’. That means his father, or an earlier ancestor, already held it. How a Jewish family in Tarsus came to have Roman citizenship is not known. Acts does not say, and these notes will not guess. Some scholars doubt Paul was a citizen at all, because his own letters never mention it; many others find that Acts gets the legal details of the period right.

The Sanhedrin was the Jewish high council in Jerusalem. The chief priests, from a few powerful families, led it with the high priest at its head, and Rome let it govern many of the people's own affairs. The commander cannot follow a quarrel about Jewish law, so he hands the question to the Jews' own council.
passages.ot:
The law Paul appeals to is Rome's, but Israel's own law also forbade punishment without a fair hearing: “Show no partiality in judging; hear both small and great alike” (Deuteronomy 1:17). And even when a guilty man was beaten, the Law set a limit to protect his dignity: “He may receive no more than forty lashes” (Deuteronomy 25:3).

God protecting his servants through outsiders has Old Testament echoes as well. Jeremiah was pulled out of the cistern because Ebed-melech the Cushite, a foreigner in the king's palace, spoke up for him (Jeremiah 38:7-13). Nehemiah travelled safely under a Persian king's letters (Nehemiah 2:7-9).
passages.hard:
Was Paul right to use his citizenship to avoid the scourge? At Philippi he took a beating with rods and spoke of his citizenship only afterward (16:22-23, 37), and he had taught the churches, “Bless those who persecute you” (Romans 12:14).

Most readers see no conflict. Paul was not refusing to suffer for Christ; he was refusing an illegal torture that served no purpose, ordered by a man who did not even know the charge. The law existed for exactly this, and asking that it be kept is not a lack of faith. Paul would go on to use the law again, appealing to Caesar (25:11), and Luke tells it without blame. Others note that Paul, in his letters, more often speaks of giving up his rights for the sake of others (1 Corinthians 9:12). Both are true of him. He used his rights when they protected the truth or other people, and laid them down when they stood in the way of the gospel. The text does not turn this into a rule for every case.
passages.asks: Paul asked a quiet question at the last moment, and the law protected him. Ask how you think about your own rights: as things to grab, as things to give up, or as tools to be used wisely for others. And notice the commander, proud of a citizenship he had paid for, meeting a prisoner who had been born with his. Ask what you are tempted to be proud of that you did not earn by being good.
